sections.directions: Directions: Read the following text. Choose the best word(s) for each numbered blank and mark A, B, C or D on the ANSWER SHEET. (10 points)

questions.analysis: warning 【线索】下句「荒原」露悲观底色 紧跟其后的一句 Some imagine that the coming work-free world will be defined by __(2)__: A few wealthy people will own all the capital, and the masses will struggle in an impoverished wasteland. 明确指出这些人想象的未来是「贫困荒原」，说明他们对技 【选项】A) boasting ✗ 色彩相反——吹嘘 boasting 是「吹嘘、自夸」，带正面或炫耀色彩，与下文 impoverished wasteland 的负面图景 B) denying ✗ 立场相反——否认 denying 是「否认」，意味着这些学者不认为技术在替代人类工作，但下文 A few wealthy people will own all the capital 正是基于「替代已发生」推演出的图景，逻辑自相矛盾。 C) warning ✓ 契合下文「贫困荒原」担忧 warning 是「警告」，与紧随其后的 the masses will struggle in an impoverished wasteland D) ensuring ✗ 色彩相反——保证 【验证】代回后整句为 academics, writers, and activists once again __(1)__ that technology is replacing human workers——「再次警告技术正在取代人类工作者」，自然引出下句的悲

inequality 【线索】冒号后「少富/众贫」即不平等 冒号后 A few wealthy people will own all the capital, and the masses will struggle in an impoverished wasteland. 描述了「少数富人占有全部资本、广大民众挣扎在贫困荒 【选项】 A) inequality ✓ 贴合「少富众贫」 inequality「不平等」精准对应冒号后「少数富人 vs 多数贫民」的两极对立，是 a few... and the masses... 这一对照结构的标准抽象词。 B) instability ✗ 强调「不稳」，与原文不符 C) unreliability ✗ 对象错位——不可靠 D) uncertainty ✗ 方向错——「不确定」 【验证】代回后 the coming work-free world will be defined by __(2)__: A few wealthy people will own all the capital, and the masses will struggle in an impoverished wasteland.

prediction 【线索】「将来时 + holds that」即预测 从句 holds that the future will be a wasteland of a different sort 用一般将来时谈论尚 未发生的事情，且与第一段开头的 People have speculated for centuries about a future without work. 中 speculated（预言/猜测）呼应，整段在罗列「关于未来的不同预测」。 【选项】A) policy ✗ 对象错——「政策」 B) guideline ✗ 对象错——「指南」 C) resolution ✗ 义近误选——「决议/决心」 D) prediction ✓ 贴合「对未来的预测」 prediction「预测」与首段 People have speculated for centuries about a future without work. 中 speculated 一脉相承，自然成为「另一种关于未来的预测」的载体。 【验证】代回后 A different and not mutually exclusive __(3)__ holds that the future will be a wasteland of a different sort, one __(4)__ by purposelessness 读为「另一种并不互斥的

characterized 【线索】前空 defined by 同义铺垫 前一句 the coming work-free world will be defined by __(2)__ 与本句 one __(4)__ by purposelessness 结构平行，前者用 defined by 表「以……定义」，后者需要语义、搭配 【选项】 A) characterized ✓ be characterized by 高频固定搭配 characterized 与 by 构成 be characterized by「以……为特征」，与上文 defined by 同向，自 B) divided ✗ 对象不合——「被分割」 divided 通常 be divided into / between，搭配的是「分成几部分」，by 后接的应是分割者， purposelessness「无目的感」无法充当「分割者」。 C) balanced ✗ 色彩相反——「被平衡」 D) measured ✗ 对象不合——「被度量」 measured 是「测量」，搭 by 时表示「以……为度量标准」，但 purposelessness 是抽象状态， 【验证】代回后 a wasteland of a different sort, one __(4)__ by purposelessness 即「另一种荒 原，以无目的感为特征」，下文紧接 Without jobs to give their lives __(5)__, people will simply become lazy and depressed. 正是这一特征的展开，整段逻辑顺承。

meaning 【线索】下文 purposelessness 反向锁定 前一句 one __(4)__ by purposelessness 已点明这种未来「以无意义为特征」；本句正是在 解释「为什么没工作就会让生活无意义」，purposelessness（无目的感）即 meaningless 【选项】A) wisdom ✗ 范围偏窄——「智慧」 「智慧」。 B) meaning ✓ 对应 purposelessness 反义 meaning「意义」与上句 purposelessness「无目的感」直接构成「失去工作→失去意义→变得 抑郁」的因果链，且 give one's life meaning 是固定搭配。 C) glory ✗ 色彩过重——「荣耀」 D) freedom ✗ 方向相反——「自由」 【验证】代回后 Without jobs to give their lives __(5)__, people will simply become lazy and purposelessness 严丝合缝，全段「无意义荒原」论展开顺畅。

Indeed 【线索】前句论断本句举证 前一句 Without jobs to give their lives __(5)__, people will simply become lazy and depressed. 是一个论断；本句 today's unemployed don't seem to be having a great time. 给的是一个支持性事实——失业者过得不好，下一句 One Gallup poll found that 20 percent of Americans who have been unemployed for at least a year report having depression 再用数据夯实。 【选项】A) Instead ✗ 方向错——「相反」 B) Indeed ✓ 「确实」承接确证 C) Thus ✗ 因果不成立——「因此」 D) Nevertheless ✗ 方向错——「然而」 【验证】代回后 __(6)__, today's unemployed don't seem to be having a great time. 读为「确

working 【线索】「unemployed」对应「working」 前文比较对象 Americans who have been unemployed for at least a year 已点明「失 业」这一身份；后半 double the rate for __(7)__ Americans 要找与「失业」直接对立的群 【选项】A) rich ✗ 维度错——「富有」 B) urban ✗ 维度错——「城市」 C) working ✓ 「在职」直接反义 D) educated ✗ 维度错——「受过教育」 educated 是教育维度；下文虽提到 poorly-educated, middle-aged people，但那是另一组研究 【验证】代回后 20 percent of Americans who have been unemployed for at least a year report having depression, double the rate for __(7)__ Americans.——「长期失业者中

explanation 【线索】「___ for X is Y」即「X 的解释是 Y」 句子 the __(8)__ for rising rates of mortality, mental-health problems, and addiction __(9)__ poorly-educated, middle-aged people is a shortage of well-paid jobs. 的逻辑 【选项】 A) explanation ✓ 「解释」契合因果框架 explanation 与 for 搭配表示「对……的解释」，且系表后 Y 正是 X 的成因，整句成为「研究表 B) requirement ✗ 方向错——「要求」 requirement 是「需求、要求」，搭 for 表示对某物的需求，但后面 Y 是「缺好工作」，并非要 C) compensation ✗ 对象错——「补偿」 D) substitute ✗ 对象错——「替代品」 substitute 表「X 的替代品是 Y」，但本句不在谈「拿什么替代 X」，而在谈 X 为什么发生，逻辑 【验证】代回后 the __(8)__ for rising rates of mortality, mental-health problems, and addiction __(9)__ poorly-educated, middle-aged people is a shortage of well-paid

among 【线索】「rates ... among + 群体」固定结构 本句 rising rates of mortality, mental-health problems, and addiction __(9)__ poorly- educated, middle-aged people 在交代这些「率」发生在哪个人群中。比例与人群之间的 【选项】A) under ✗ 搭配不当——「在……下」 B) beyond ✗ 义反——「超越」 C) alongside ✗ 对象错——「与……并行」 D) among ✓ 「在……中」契合统计框架 among「在……之中」是 rates/rises among + 人群的固定搭配，完美贴合「这些率在受教育不 【验证】代回后 rising rates of mortality, mental-health problems, and addiction __(9)__ poorly-educated, middle-aged people 即「在受教育不足的中年人群中，死亡率、心理

worry about 【线索】前文负面图景定调「担忧」 整段 purposelessness、lazy and depressed、depression、rising rates of mortality, mental-health problems, and addiction 已铺陈无工作未来的种种负面后果；本句以 Perhaps this is why 总结众人为何会有某种反应，反应方向必为负面。 【选项】A) leave behind ✗ 方向错——「抛在身后」 leave behind「抛下、置之不理」与「担忧未来」方向相反，且语义上无法 leave behind 一种尚 B) make up ✗ 对象错——「编造/弥补」 C) worry about ✓ 「担忧」契合负面铺陈 D) set aside ✗ 方向错——「搁置一旁」 【验证】代回后 Perhaps this is why many __(10)__ the agonizing dullness of a jobless future.

necessarily 【线索】本句作者立场反转 本句 But it doesn't __(11)__ follow from findings like these that a world without work would be filled with unease. 用 But 与前段相反——前文虽然举了一堆负面证据，但作者 【选项】A) statistically ✗ 维度过窄——「统计上」 B) occasionally ✗ 频率不合——「偶尔」 C) necessarily ✓ 「未必必然推出」 necessarily 与 doesn't follow 构成 not necessarily follow「并不必然推出」的高频反驳句式， D) economically ✗ 维度错——「经济上」 【验证】代回后 But it doesn't __(11)__ follow from findings like these that a world without work would be filled with unease. 即「但这些发现并不必然推出无工作世界会充满不 安」，恰好引出下文 Such visions are based on the __(12)__ of being unemployed in a society built on the concept of employment. 的进一步反驳，第三段反转立得住。

downsides 【线索】前文铺陈失业的负面后果 前段全在罗列失业的负面后果（depression、rising rates of mortality 等），本句 Such visions are based on the __(12)__ of being unemployed in a society built on the concept of employment. 在解释「悲观派为何如此论证」——他们看到的是失业的 「弊端」。 【选项】A) chances ✗ 对象错——「机会」 chances「机会」与悲观图景毫无关联，无法解释为何 such visions 是悲观的。 B) downsides ✓ 「弊端」与悲观图景因果 C) benefits ✗ 色彩相反——「好处」 benefits「好处」与悲观图景的负面色彩完全相反，无法解释为何 such visions 充满悲观。 D) principles ✗ 维度错——「原则」 【验证】代回后 Such visions are based on the __(12)__ of being unemployed in a society built on the concept of employment.——「这些悲观图景是基于『在以就业为本的社会中失 业』的弊端」，恰好承接前段失业负面后果，又为下文 In the __(13)__ of work, a society designed with other ends in mind could __(14)__ strikingly different circumstances

absence 【线索】下文「另作设计的社会」 本句 In the __(13)__ of work, a society designed with other ends in mind could __(14)__ strikingly different circumstances for the future of labor and leisure. 在勾 勒「没有工作时」的反事实情景；与全文 a future without work（无工作的未来）反复 【选项】 A) absence ✓ 「在工作缺失时」契合全文 absence 与全文反复出现的 a future without work、a world without work 完全一致，「在工 B) height ✗ 方向错——「鼎盛」 C) face ✗ 对象错——「面对」 face 在 in the face of N 里多表「面对挑战/威胁」，搭 work 时语义勉强且与全段反事实假设 D) course ✗ 时间向错——「过程中」 course 在 in the course of N 里指「在……过程中」，表示工作仍在进行，与「无工作的反事实」 【验证】代回后 In the __(13)__ of work, a society designed with other ends in mind could __(14)__ strikingly different circumstances for the future of labor and leisure. 即「在

yield 【线索】前文反事实假设结果出处 本句逻辑链是「a society designed with other ends in mind」（一个另作设计的社会） 【选项】A) disturb ✗ 色彩相反——「扰乱」 B) restore ✗ 方向错——「恢复」 restore「恢复」要求宾语是失去的旧物，但宾语 strikingly different circumstances 强调「全 C) exclude ✗ 方向错——「排除」 D) yield ✓ 「产生」契合假设导果 yield 表「产生、带来」，yield ... circumstances 自然表达「这种社会会带来截然不同的劳逸局 【验证】代回后 a society designed with other ends in mind could __(14)__ strikingly different circumstances for the future of labor and leisure.——「一个以其他目的为导向设计的

virtue 【线索】下句引言揭示「美德被夸大」 紧接下文 Many jobs are boring, degrading, unhealthy, and a waste of human 【选项】A) model ✗ 对象错——「模型」 B) practice ✗ 维度错——「实践」 practice「实践、惯例」描述工作的形式，不是被「吹过头」的对象——overblown 通常修饰被高 C) virtue ✓ 「美德」被引言精确打脸 virtue「美德、价值」与紧随的批评 boring, degrading, unhealthy 完全对照——「工作很有价 D) hardship ✗ 色彩相反——「艰辛」 【验证】代回后 Today, the __(15)__ of work may be a bit overblown. 即「如今工作的可贵之处也 许被吹得过头了」，与紧随引言 Many jobs are boring, degrading, unhealthy, and a waste of human potential 形成「论点—例证」的完美对接。

scarce 【线索】「闲暇用来平衡工作」反推「稀缺」 下半句 people use their free time to counterbalance the intellectual and emotional __(17)__ of their jobs.「人们用闲暇时间平衡工作的认知与情绪压力」隐含「闲暇时间不 工作」。 【选项】A) tricky ✗ 维度错——「棘手」 B) lengthy ✗ 方向相反——「冗长」 C) mysterious ✗ 对象错——「神秘」 mysterious「神秘」与闲暇时间的可用性无关，无法服务于 because 因果。 D) scarce ✓ 「稀缺」贴合因果 【验证】代回后 because leisure time is relatively __(16)__ for most workers, people use their free time to counterbalance the intellectual and emotional __(17)__ of their jobs. 即 下文 In a world in which I don't have to work, I might feel rather different 的假设衔接

demands 【线索】「平衡」要求宾语是「负担」 本句 people use their free time to counterbalance the intellectual and emotional __(17)__ of their jobs. 既然要用闲暇去「抵消」工作的某种东西，被抵消的必是工作的负 【选项】 A) demands ✓ 「需求/负担」契合 counterbalance demands「需求、要求」指工作对人智力与情绪的索取，是 counterbalance 的天然宾语，「平 B) standards ✗ 对象错——「标准」 C) qualities ✗ 色彩错——「品质」 D) threats ✗ 色彩过重——「威胁」 threats「威胁」语气过重，且 intellectual/emotional threats 搭配生硬；下文 I often feel __(18)__ 描绘的是累、不是被威胁。 【验证】代回后 people use their free time to counterbalance the intellectual and emotional __(17)__ of their jobs.——「人们用闲暇时间来抵消工作对认知与情绪的需求」，自然引出

tired 【线索】「a hard day's work」直接定调 本句 When I come home from a hard day's work, I often feel __(18)__ 中 hard day's 【选项】A) ignored ✗ 对象错——「被忽视」 ignored「被忽视」涉及他人对自己的态度，与 hard day's work 后的体感无关。 B) tired ✓ 「疲惫」与 hard day's work 标准搭配 tired「疲惫」是 a hard day's work 之后最自然的情感状态，与上文「智力与情绪需求」消耗完 C) confused ✗ 维度错——「困惑」 confused「困惑」描述认知状态，hard day's work 不必然导致困惑，且下文设想是「不那么累就 D) starved ✗ 维度错——「饥饿」 【验证】代回后 When I come home from a hard day's work, I often feel __(18)__ 即「辛苦工作 一天后回到家，我常感到疲惫」，与下文 In a world in which I don't have to work, I might feel rather different 的反事实假设「不用工作时可能感觉很不同」形成完美对照。

into 【线索】本句框架内即可定 本句 throw himself __(19)__ a hobby or a passion project with the intensity usually reserved for __(20)__ matters 后接 a hobby「爱好」与 the intensity「强烈程度」，框架 【选项】A) off ✗ 搭配错——「脱开」 off 在 throw off 里表「摆脱、抛弃」，与「投入爱好」语义相反。 B) against ✗ 搭配错——「对抗」 against 表「抵抗、反对」，throw oneself against 不构成「全身心投入」语义。 C) behind ✗ 搭配错——「在……之后」 behind 通常表位置或时间「在后」，throw oneself behind 不是固定表达，且与「投入」语义 D) into ✓ 「投入」铁配 into into 与 throw oneself 构成 throw oneself into N 的固定搭配，表「全身心投入」，恰对应下 【验证】代回后 throw himself __(19)__ a hobby or a passion project with the intensity usually reserved for __(20)__ matters 即「全身心投入一项爱好或激情项目，强度堪比平时只用于

professional 【线索】全文「工作 vs 闲暇」基调 整段 the intellectual and emotional __(17)__ of their jobs、When I come home from a hard day's work 都在围绕「工作」与「闲暇」对照；此处「平时只留给 ___ matters」必 然回到 job/work 这一面，即 professional 「职业/工作的」。 【选项】A) technological ✗ 对象错——「技术性」 B) professional ✓ 「职业事」对照爱好 professional「职业的、工作相关的」与 a hobby「爱好」形成「正经工作 vs 业余爱好」对 C) educational ✗ 对象错——「教育的」 educational「教育的」与「工作 vs 闲暇」主对照线无关。 D) interpersonal ✗ 对象错——「人际」 【验证】代回后 throw himself __(19)__ a hobby or a passion project with the intensity usually reserved for __(20)__ matters 即「以平时只留给职业事的强度投入到爱好或激情项目 OVERVIEW · 通读建境 心 A few wealthy people will own all the capital, and the masses will struggle in an impoverished wasteland. 与 Without jobs to give their lives __(5)__, people will simply become lazy and depressed.，再以 But it doesn't __(11)__ follow from findings like these that a world without work would be filled with unease. 转折，给出作者基调——若社会重 全文呈四段递进。第一段提出 a future without work 与「不平等荒原」的悲观图景；第二 段补出另一种「无意义荒原」并用 One Gallup poll found that 20 percent of Americans who have been unemployed for at least a year report having depression 的失业抑郁数据 佐证；第三段以 But it doesn't __(11)__ follow from findings like these 关键转折反驳，提出 a society designed with other ends in mind 的可能，并借专家话 Many jobs are boring, degrading, unhealthy, and a waste of human potential 重估「工作的美德」；第四段从 「闲暇稀缺」推到 In a world in which I don't have to work, I might feel rather different 的 SENTENCE INSIGHTS · 句子精讲 5 Today is no different, with academics, writers, and activists once agai...

sections.title: 阅读理解
sections.directions: Read the following four texts. Answer the questions after each text by choosing A, B, C or D. Mark your answers on the ANSWER SHEET. (40 points)

blocks.content: Every Saturday morning, at 9 am, more than 50,000 runners set off to run 5km around their local park. The Parkrun phenomenon began with a dozen friends and has inspired 400 events in the UK and more abroad. Events are free, staffed by thousands of volunteers. Runners range from four years old to grandparents; their times range from Andrew Baddeley's world record 13 minutes 48 seconds up to an hour. Parkrun is succeeding where London's Olympic "legacy" is failing. Ten years ago on Monday, it was announced that the Games of the 30th Olympiad would be in London. Planning documents pledged that the great legacy of the Games would be to lever a nation of sport lovers away from their couches. The population would be fitter, healthier and produce more winners. It has not happened. The number of adults doing weekly sport did rise, by nearly 2 million in the run-up to 2012 – but the general population was growing faster. Worse, the numbers are now falling at an accelerating rate. The opposition claims primary school pupils doing at least two hours of sport a week have nearly halved. Obesity has risen among adults and children. Official retrospections continue as to why London 2012 failed to "inspire a generation." The success of Parkrun offers answers. Parkun is not a race but a time trial: Your only competitor is the clock. The ethos welcomes anybody. There is as much joy over a puffed-out first-timer being clapped over the line as there is about top talent shining. The Olympic bidders, by contrast, wanted to get more people doing sport and to produce more elite athletes. The dual aim was mixed up: The stress on success over taking part was intimidating for newcomers. Indeed, there is something a little absurd in the state getting involved in the planning of such a fundamentally "grassroots" concept as community sports associations. If there is a role for government, it should really be getting involved in providing common goods – making sure there is space for playing fields and the money to pave tennis and netball courts, and encouraging the provision of all these activities in schools. But successive governments have presided over selling green spaces, squeezing money from local authorities and declining attention on sport in education. Instead of wordy, worthy strategies, future governments need to do more to provide the conditions for sport to thrive. Or at least not make them worse.

With so much focus on children's use of screens, it's easy for parents to forget about their own screen use. "Tech is designed to really suck you in," says Jenny Radesky in her study of digital play, "and digital products are there to promote maximal engagement. It makes it hard to disengage, and leads to a lot of bleed-over into the family routine." Radesky has studied the use of mobile phones and tablets at mealtimes by giving mother-child pairs a food- testing exercise. She found that mothers who used devices during the exercise started 20 per cent fewer verbal and 39 per cent fewer nonverbal interactions with their children. During a separate observation, she saw that phones became a source of tension in the family. Parents would be looking at their emails while the children would be making excited bids for their attention. Infants are wired to look at parents' faces to try to understand their world, and if those faces are blank and unresponsive – as they often are when absorbed in a device – it can be extremely disconcerting for the children. Radesky cites the "still face experiment" devised by developmental psychologist Ed Tronick in the 1970s. In it, a mother is asked to interact with her child in a normal way before putting on a blank expression and not giving them any visual social feedback: The child becomes increasingly distressed as she tries to capture her mother's attention. "Parents don't have to be exquisitely present at all times, but there needs to be a balance and parents need to be responsive and sensitive to a child's verbal or nonverbal expressions of an emotional need," says Radesky. On the other hand, Tronick himself is concerned that the worries about kids' use of screens are born out of an "oppressive ideology that demands that parents should always be interacting" with their children: "It's based on a somewhat fantasised, very white, very upper-middle-class ideology that says if you're failing to expose your child to 30,000 words you are neglecting them." Tronick believes that just because a child isn't learning from the screen doesn't mean there's no value to it – particularly if it gives parents time to have a shower, do housework or simply have a break from their child. Parents, he says, can get a lot out of using their devices to speak to a friend or get some work out of the way. This can make them feel happier, which lets them be more available to their child the rest of the time.

Today, widespread social pressure to immediately go to college in conjunction with increasingly high expectations in a fast-moving world often causes students to completely overlook the possibility of taking a gap year. After all, if everyone you know is going to college in the fall, it seems silly to stay back a year, doesn't it? And after going to school for 12 years, it doesn't feel natural to spend a year doing something that isn't academic. But while this may be true, it's not a good enough reason to condemn gap years. There's always a constant fear of falling behind everyone else on the socially perpetuated "race to the finish line," whether that be toward graduate school, medical school or a lucrative career. But despite common misconceptions, a gap year does not hinder the success of academic pursuits – in fact, it probably enhances it. Studies from the United States and Australia show that students who take a gap year are generally better prepared for and perform better in college than those who do not. Rather than pulling students back, a gap year pushes them ahead by preparing them for independence, new responsibilities and environmental changes – all things that first-year students often struggle with the most. Gap year experiences can lessen the blow when it comes to adjusting to college and being thrown into a brand new environment, making it easier to focus on academics and activities rather than acclimation blunders. If you're not convinced of the inherent value in taking a year off to explore interests, then consider its financial impact on future academic choices. According to the National Center for Education Statistics, nearly 80 percent of college students end up changing their majors at least once. This isn't surprising, considering the basic mandatory high school curriculum leaves students with a poor understanding of the vast academic possibilities that await them in college. Many students find themselves listing one major on their college applications, but switching to another after taking college classes. It's not necessarily a bad thing, but depending on the school, it can be costly to make up credits after switching too late in the game. At Boston College, for example, you would have to complete an extra year were you to switch to the nursing school from another department. Taking a gap year to figure things out initially can help prevent stress and save money later on.

Though often viewed as a problem for western states, the growing frequency of wildfires is a national concern because of its impact on federal tax dollars, says Professor Max Moritz, a specialist in fire ecology and management. In 2015, the US Forest Service for the first time spent more than half of its $5.5 billion annual budget fighting fires – nearly double the percentage it spent on such efforts 20 years ago. In effect, fewer federal funds today are going towards the agency's other work – such as forest conservation, watershed and cultural resources management, and infrastructure upkeep – that affect the lives of all Americans. Another nationwide concern is whether public funds from other agencies are going into construction in fire- prone districts. As Moritz puts it, how often are federal dollars building homes that are likely to be lost to a wildfire? "It's already a huge problem from a public expenditure perspective for the whole country," he says. "We need to take a magnifying glass to that. Like, 'Wait a minute, is this OK?' Do we want instead to redirect those funds to concentrate on lower-hazard parts of the landscape?" Such a view would require a corresponding shift in the way US society today views fire, researchers say. For one thing, conversations about wildfires need to be more inclusive. Over the past decade, the focus has been on climate change – how the warming of the Earth from greenhouse gases is leading to conditions that worsen fires. While climate is a key element, Moritz says, it shouldn't come at the expense of the rest of the equation. "The human systems and the landscapes we live on are linked, and the interactions go both ways," he says. Failing to recognize that, he notes, leads to "an overly simplified view of what the solutions might be. Our perception of the problem and of what the solution is becomes very limited." At the same time, people continue to treat fire as an event that needs to be wholly controlled and unleashed only out of necessity, says Professor Balch at the University of Colorado. But acknowledging fire's inevitable presence in human life is an attitude crucial to developing the laws, policies, and practices that make it as safe as possible, she says. "We've disconnected ourselves from living with fire," Balch says. "It is really important to understand and try and tease out what is the human connection with fire today."

sections.title: 新题型
sections.directions: Part B Directions:Read the following text and match each of the numbered items in the left column to its corresponding information in the right column. There are two extra choices in the right column. Mark your answers on the ANSWER SHEET. (10 points)

blocks.content: The decline in American manufacturing is a common refrain, particularly from Donald Trump. "We don't make anything anymore," he told Fox News, while defending his own made-in-Mexico clothing line. Without question, manufacturing has taken a significant hit during recent decades, and further trade deals raise questions about whether new shocks could hit manufacturing. But there is also a different way to look at the data. Across the country, factory owners are now grappling with a new challenge: Instead of having too many workers, they may end up with too few. Despite trade competition and outsourcing, American manufacturing still needs to replace tens of thousands of retiring boomers every year. Millennials may not be that interested in taking their place. Other industries are recruiting them with similar or better pay. For factory owners, it all adds up to stiff competition for workers – and upward pressure on wages. "They're harder to find and they have job offers," says Jay Dunwell, president of Wolverine Coil Spring, a family-owned firm, "They may be coming [into the workforce], but they've been plucked by other industries that are also doing as well as manufacturing." Mr. Dunwell has begun bringing high school juniors to the factory so they can get exposed to its culture. At RoMan Manufacturing, a maker of electrical transformers and welding equipment that his father cofounded in 1980, Robert Roth keeps a close eye on the age of his nearly 200 workers. Five are retiring this year. Mr. Roth has three community-college students enrolled in a work-placement program, with a starting wage of $13 an hour that rises to $17 after two years. At a worktable inside the transformer plant, young Jason Stenquist looks flustered by the copper coils he's trying to assemble and the arrival of two visitors. It's his first week on the job. Asked about his choice of career, he says at high school he considered medical school before switching to electrical engineering. "I love working with tools. I love creating," he says. But to win over these young workers, manufacturers have to clear another major hurdle: parents, who lived through the worst US economic downturn since the Great Depression, telling them to avoid the factory. Millennials "remember their father and mother both were laid off. They blame it on the manufacturing recession," says Birgit Klohs, chief executive of The Right Place, a business development agency for western Michigan. These concerns aren't misplaced: Employment in manufacturing has fallen from 17 million in 1970 to 12 million in 2015. When the recovery began, worker shortages first appeared in the high-skilled trades. Now shortages are appearing at the mid-skill levels. "The gap is between the jobs that take no skills and those that require a lot of skill," says Rob Spohr, a business professor at Montcalm Community College. "There're enough people to fill the jobs at McDonalds and other places where you don't need to have much skill. It's that gap in between, and that's where the problem is." Julie Parks of Grand Rapids Community College points to another key to luring Millennials into manufacturing: a work/life balance. While their parents were content to work long hours, young people value flexibility. "Overtime is not attractive to this generation. They really want to live their lives," she says. because he loves working with tools.
